entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To recover quickly and return to your normal level after a failure, illness, injury or bad period.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business news and everyday talk: people, teams, markets and economies *bounce back*. It is intransitive; add *from* for the problem: *bounce back from an injury, a loss, a breakup*. It sounds positive and suggests energy and resilience; for a slow, difficult recovery, *recover* is more accurate.
entries.pattern: bounce back (from a loss / an injury / a setback)
examples: She lost her job in March, but she **bounced back** and found a better one by summer.
After two straight losses, the team **bounced back** with a big win at home on Saturday.
Kids usually **bounce back** from a stomach bug within a day or two.

drill.sentence: Everyone has a bad game now and then. What matters is how fast you {{bounce back}}.
drill.hint: return to your normal level after a setback (not *recover* or *rebound*)

entries.related: *recover* — neutral, can be slow; *rebound* — similar, common for prices and markets; *get over something* — stop being affected by an illness or a loss; *comeback* — the noun for a return to success.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become physically and emotionally exhausted, and lose your motivation, after working too hard or under stress for too long.
entries.usage: Very common in talk about work, school, caregiving and sports. It is intransitive (*Many nurses are burning out*), the adjective is *burned out* (*burnt out* is also used), and the noun is *burnout*. *Burn yourself out* stresses that your own habits caused it.
entries.pattern: burn out; be / get burned out; burn yourself out
examples: After six years of night shifts in the ER, she **burned out** and left nursing.
A lot of young athletes **burn out** before college because they train year-round.
Caring for her mother alone, Lisa was completely **burned out** by the end of the year.

drill.sentence: My daughter has school, soccer, piano and a tutor every day. I'm worried she's going to {{burn out}}.
drill.hint: get completely exhausted from doing too much (not *crash* or *break down*)

entries.related: *wear yourself out* — get very tired, often for a short time; *be run down* — tired and slightly ill; *burnout* — the noun, very common in talk about work.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To increase gradually, little by little, until there is a lot of something.
entries.usage: Used for things that collect or grow slowly, often unwanted ones: *dust, debt, pressure, tension, traffic*. In this sense it is intransitive and often in the progressive or perfect: *Tension had been building up for weeks.* The transitive *build something up* means develop it on purpose: *build up savings, strength, a business*.
entries.pattern: dust / debt / tension / traffic builds up; build up savings
examples: Dust **builds up** behind the fridge, so pull it out and clean back there once a year.
Tension between the two brothers had been **building up** for years before the fight at Thanksgiving.
Credit card debt can **build up** fast if you only make the minimum payment.

drill.sentence: Leave before three. After that, traffic {{builds up}} and the drive takes twice as long.
drill.hint: gradually gets heavier (not *picks up* or *gets bad*)

entries.related: *pile up* — similar, for things that collect, like work, bills or snow; *accumulate* — formal; *build on* — use earlier work as a base.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To use an earlier success, idea or piece of work as a base and develop it further.
entries.usage: Common at work, in education, sports and news: *build on this success, last year's results, earlier research, our strengths*. It is inseparable (*build on it*) and sounds positive and forward-looking. *Build upon* means the same and is more formal.
entries.pattern: build on a success / earlier work / your strengths
examples: After a strong first season, the coach wants to **build on** what worked and make the playoffs.
This year's Spanish class **builds on** the basics you learned last year.
The new study **builds on** earlier work showing that exercise improves sleep.

drill.sentence: The restaurant had a great first year, and now the owners want to {{build on}} that success by opening a second location.
drill.hint: use as a base for further growth (not *capitalize on* or *cash in on*)

entries.related: *expand on* — explain an idea in more detail; *capitalize on* — use a chance to gain an advantage; *build up* — increase gradually.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To give more details or a fuller explanation about something you or someone else has already mentioned.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, interviews, classes and question-and-answer sessions: *Could you expand on that?* It is inseparable and is followed by a point, an idea or a comment, often *that* or *what you said*. *Elaborate on* means the same and is a little more formal.
entries.pattern: expand on a point / an idea / what someone said
examples: That's an interesting point. Could you **expand on** it a little?
My professor liked my essay but asked me to **expand on** the second point.
A team spokesperson declined to **expand on** the coach's comments about the trade.

drill.sentence: At the book signing, a reader asked the author to {{expand on}} what she meant by "quiet courage."
drill.hint: explain in more detail (not *elaborate on* or *clarify*)

entries.related: *elaborate on* — same, more formal; *go into* — discuss in detail (*I won't go into that*); *clarify* — make something clear, not necessarily longer.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To understand how someone feels because you have had similar experiences yourself.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often with *can* or *can't*: *I can totally relate to that.* The object can be a person, a character, a song or a situation, and *I can relate* with no object is a common reply. Don't confuse it with *be related to*, which means be family or be connected.
entries.pattern: (can / can't) relate to someone / something; I can relate.
examples: My parents never lived abroad, so they can't really **relate to** what I'm going through.
A lot of viewers **relate to** the main character, a single mom working two jobs.
"My toddler hasn't slept through the night in weeks." "Oh, I can **relate**."

drill.sentence: Teenagers often feel that their parents can't {{relate to}} them, even though their parents were teenagers once too.
drill.hint: know how they feel from similar experience (not *connect with* or *identify with*)

entries.related: *identify with* — feel that you are like someone; *empathize with* — more formal, understand feelings even without the same experience; *sympathize with* — feel sorry for someone.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To accept something that is less good than what you wanted, because you can't get the better thing.
entries.usage: Common in talk about jobs, homes, relationships, prices and food: *settle for less, second place, a smaller apartment*. It is often used as advice in the negative (*Don't settle for less*), and *settle* alone means the same in relationships and careers: *Don't settle.* Don't confuse it with *settle on*, which means finally choose.
entries.pattern: settle for + less / second place / something cheaper
examples: They wanted a house with a big yard but had to **settle for** a two-bedroom condo.
The restaurant was out of salmon, so I **settled for** the chicken.
You're smart and kind. Don't **settle for** someone who doesn't treat you well.

drill.sentence: Tickets for the Saturday show were gone, so we had to {{settle for}} Tuesday night, which wasn't ideal.
drill.hint: accept as a less good option (not *go with* or *make do with*)

entries.related: *make do with* — manage with something that is not good enough; *settle on* — finally choose; *compromise on* — accept less to reach an agreement.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To begin something again from the very beginning, usually because the first attempt failed or went wrong.
entries.usage: The usual American phrase; British speakers more often say *start again*. It is usually intransitive (*Let's start over*), but an object can go in the middle: *I had to start the whole essay over.* It can also mean begin a new life somewhere: *start over in a new city*.
entries.pattern: start over (from scratch); start something over
examples: I forgot to save the file, so I had to **start over** from scratch.
After a fire destroyed their home, the family moved to Ohio to **start over**.
The kids kept arguing about the rules, so we **started** the game **over**.

drill.sentence: The cake was burned on the bottom, so I threw it out and {{started over}}.
drill.hint: began again from zero (the usual American phrase)

entries.related: *start again* — the same, more common in British English; *start from scratch* — begin with nothing prepared; *redo* — do one task again.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To find someone or something after a long search, often by following several clues or sources.
entries.usage: Common with old friends, relatives, rare items, documents and suspects: *track down a copy, the owner, the source of a leak*. A noun object usually follows *down*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *I finally tracked her down.* It stresses effort and persistence, unlike plain *find*.
entries.pattern: track down a person / a copy / the source; track someone down
examples: It took me three years to **track down** my birth mother.
I finally **tracked down** a copy of the out-of-print cookbook my mom grew up with.
Police **tracked** the driver **down** using video from a neighbor's doorbell camera.

drill.sentence: It took the mechanic a week to {{track down}} a part for my 1972 pickup truck.
drill.hint: find after a long search (not *locate*)

entries.related: *hunt down* — search hard, often for a person who is hiding; *find* — neutral, no effort implied; *look for* — search, without saying you succeeded.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start or continue doing something that was planned, often after getting permission or after a delay.
entries.usage: Very common as a way to give permission: *Sure, go ahead.* In news and at work it means proceed: *The concert will go ahead despite the rain*, *go ahead with the plan*. *Go ahead and* + verb is very common in American speech and makes an action sound relaxed: *I'll go ahead and order.*
entries.pattern: Go ahead.; go ahead (with something); go ahead and + verb
examples: "Can I borrow your charger for a minute?" "Sure, **go ahead**."
The parade **went ahead** as planned, even though it rained all morning.
I'll **go ahead** and book the hotel unless you have a better idea.

drill.sentence: The movie's about to start, so {{go ahead}} and grab seats; I'll get the popcorn.
drill.hint: don't wait for me (phrasal verb, before *and* + verb)

entries.related: *proceed* — formal; *carry on* — continue after a pause; the noun *the go-ahead* means permission: *We got the go-ahead.*

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To try hard to get or achieve something, such as a job, a prize or a goal, especially when success is not certain.
entries.usage: Very common as encouragement: *Go for it!* means try it and take the chance. It is used for jobs, promotions, medals, records and big life plans: *go for the job, gold, a world record*. It is inseparable; in other contexts *go for* can also mean choose, as in *I'll go for the salad*.
entries.pattern: go for a job / a promotion / gold; Go for it!
examples: The marketing director job just opened up, and I think I'm going to **go for** it.
She's **going for** her third straight title at this weekend's tournament.
"Should I ask her out?" "Absolutely. **Go for it**!"

drill.sentence: My brother is {{going for}} a spot on the Olympic swim team, so he trains six hours a day.
drill.hint: making a serious attempt to win (not *trying for*, *aiming for* or *competing for*)

entries.related: *aim for* — have as a target; *apply for* — formally ask for a job; *go after* — try hard to get something, often a job or a client.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To do something wrong or against the rules without being caught or punished.
entries.usage: Common in speech about kids, cheating, crime and broken rules, often in warnings: *You won't get away with this.* It is inseparable and takes a noun or an *-ing* form: *get away with lying*. *Can I get away with* + *-ing* asks whether something slightly improper will be accepted: *Can I get away with wearing sneakers?*
entries.pattern: get away with + noun / -ing; get away with it
examples: He parks in the fire lane every morning and somehow always **gets away with** it.
My little sister **gets away with** everything because she's the baby of the family.
The company **got away with** dumping waste into the river for years before anyone noticed.

drill.sentence: Everyone saw him copy the answers, so there's no way he's going to {{get away with}} it.
drill.hint: avoid punishment for

entries.related: *get away with murder* — informal exaggeration, do whatever you like without punishment; *get off easy* — receive a light punishment after being caught.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To prepare or build something by collecting and combining different parts, ideas or people.
entries.usage: Very common for plans, meals, teams, presentations and furniture: *put together a proposal, a team, a quick dinner*. A noun object usually follows *together*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *put it together*. It sounds practical and informal, and it often suggests the work was done quickly: *I put together a few slides.*
entries.pattern: put together a plan / a team / a meal / some slides
examples: It took us four hours to **put together** the new bookshelf, and we still had three screws left over.
I'll **put together** a few slides for Monday's meeting.
The neighbors **put together** a box of meals and gift cards for the family whose house burned down.

drill.sentence: My sister {{put together}} a photo album of our trip for Mom's birthday.
drill.hint: created by collecting and arranging pieces (not *made* or *compiled*)

entries.related: *assemble* — more formal, especially for furniture or machines; *throw together* — make quickly and carelessly; *put it all together* — also means finally understand by combining facts.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To cancel a planned event or activity, or to decide to stop one that has already started.
entries.usage: Common for weddings, strikes, games, searches and deals: *call off the wedding, the search, the strike*. A noun object can go before or after *off*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *They called it off.* It is often passive: *The game was called off because of rain.*
entries.pattern: call off a wedding / a game / a search; call it off
examples: The two companies **called off** the merger after months of talks.
Saturday's game was **called off** because of lightning in the area.
After three days, the Coast Guard **called off** the search for the missing fishing boat.

drill.sentence: We'd planned a camping trip, but with heavy snow in the forecast, we {{called it off}}.
drill.hint: decided it wouldn't happen after all (not *canceled it* or *scrapped it*)

entries.related: *cancel* — neutral, for anything planned; *postpone* or *put off* — move to a later time; *scrap* — informal, drop a plan completely.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To end someone's employment because the employer has too little work or money, not because the worker did anything wrong.
entries.usage: Common in news and everyday talk about the economy: *lay off workers, half the staff*. It is very often passive (*I got laid off*), and the noun is *layoff*. A noun object can go before or after *off*; a pronoun goes in the middle: *They laid him off.*
entries.pattern: lay off workers / staff; get laid off
examples: The plant **laid off** three hundred workers after losing its biggest contract.
My dad got **laid off** last spring, so money's been tight at home.
Rather than **lay** anyone **off**, the bakery cut everyone's hours for the winter.

drill.sentence: After twenty years at the same company, my uncle was {{laid off}} with two weeks' notice.
drill.hint: dismissed because there wasn't enough work or money (not *fired* or *let go*)

mistake.wrong: The factory closed, so I was fired along with everyone else.
mistake.right: The factory closed, so I was laid off along with everyone else.
mistake.why: *Fired* suggests you were dismissed for poor work or bad behavior; *laid off* says it was not your fault.

entries.related: *fire* — dismiss for poor work or behavior; *let someone go* — a softer phrase for either; *furlough* — send workers home without pay for a period.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To leave an important job or position, such as CEO, coach or chair, usually by your own choice.
entries.usage: Common in news about leaders and managers: *step down as CEO, from the board, after twenty years*. It is intransitive; use *as* + the role or *from* + the position or organization. It sounds more neutral and dignified than *quit*, and less formal than *resign*.
entries.pattern: step down (as CEO / from the board)
examples: After twelve years in charge, the coach **stepped down** to spend more time with his family.
The CEO will **step down** at the end of the year, and the board is looking for a replacement.
My mom **stepped down** as president of the PTA when she went back to work full-time.

drill.sentence: After the scandal, the hospital's director agreed to {{step down}} at the end of the month.
drill.hint: give up the top job (not *resign* or *quit*)

entries.related: *resign* — more formal, and can be forced; *step aside* — leave a role so someone else can take it, often for a time; *retire* — stop working because of age.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To close a business, factory or service, permanently or for a time, or to stop a machine or system from operating.
entries.usage: Common in news about factories, stores, roads and websites: *shut down a plant, a highway, a website*. It works with or without an object (*The plant shut down last year*), and a pronoun goes in the middle: *shut it down*. The noun is *shutdown*.
entries.pattern: shut down a plant / a store / a highway; shut it down
examples: The owners **shut down** the restaurant after the rent nearly doubled.
The city is **shutting down** two lanes of the highway for repairs this weekend.
Health inspectors **shut** the food truck **down** after finding mice in the kitchen.

drill.sentence: Don't {{shut down}} your laptop yet; it's still installing an update.
drill.hint: power off completely (not *turn off* or *switch off*)

entries.related: *close down* — very similar; *shut off* — stop a machine, the water or the power; *go out of business* — fail and close.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To keep money, time or things for a particular purpose and not use them for anything else.
entries.usage: Common in personal finance, planning and official budgets: *set aside money for taxes, an hour a day, land for a park*. A noun object usually follows *aside*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *set it aside*. *Put aside* means the same and is more informal; *set aside* can also mean ignore for now: *set aside your doubts*.
entries.pattern: set aside money / time / an hour (for something)
examples: I **set aside** two hundred dollars every month for car repairs.
We **set aside** Sunday afternoons for family time, and nobody's allowed on their phone.
Could you **set** a copy **aside** for me? I'll pick it up after work.

drill.sentence: The county {{set aside}} two hundred acres along the river for a nature preserve.
drill.hint: kept for one special use (not *earmarked* or *reserved*)

entries.related: *put aside* — same, more informal; *save* — more general; *earmark* — formal, mainly for money in budgets.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To prevent someone or something from making progress or reaching their full potential.
entries.usage: Common in talk about careers, school, fears and relationships: *Fear held her back*, *What's holding you back?* The subject is often a fear, a habit or a problem, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *hold him back*. In American schools, *be held back* also means repeat a grade.
entries.pattern: X holds someone back; What's holding you back?
examples: Her fear of public speaking **held** her **back** at work for years.
You've got the money and the time, so what's **holding** you **back**?
Slow internet is **holding back** small businesses in rural areas.

drill.sentence: He's a talented singer, but his shyness is really {{holding him back}}.
drill.hint: stopping him from making progress (not *limiting him*)

entries.related: *keep someone from doing something* — prevent it; *get in the way of something* — be an obstacle; *hold back* without an object — not say or do all you could: *Don't hold back.*

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To suddenly become very successful or popular, often after a slow start.
entries.usage: Common for businesses, careers, products, songs and trends: *Her career really took off after that movie.* It is intransitive in this sense and often comes with *really* or *finally*. The same verb also means leave the ground (a plane) or leave quickly, so context matters.
entries.pattern: a business / a career / a trend takes off
examples: Their little hot sauce business **took off** after a food blogger posted about it.
Electric bikes have really **taken off** in our city; you see them everywhere now.
His acting career didn't **take off** until he was in his forties.

drill.sentence: Nobody bought the board game at first, but sales {{took off}} once a famous streamer started playing it.
drill.hint: suddenly grew very fast (not *picked up* or *skyrocketed*)

entries.related: *catch on* — become popular, often gradually; *blow up* — informal, become popular very quickly online; *pick up* — improve or increase, less dramatic.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To finally agree to something or stop resisting, after refusing or arguing for some time.
entries.usage: Common in talk about kids, negotiations and temptations: *We finally gave in and got a dog.* It is intransitive; add *to* for the person, demand or feeling you yield to: *give in to pressure, demands, temptation*. Don't confuse it with *give up*, which means stop trying.
entries.pattern: give in (to pressure / demands / temptation / someone)
examples: The kids begged for a puppy for two years, and we finally **gave in**.
The company **gave in** to the workers' demands after a three-week strike.
I was doing so well on my diet, but I **gave in** and ordered the fries.

drill.sentence: My toddler screamed for candy at the checkout, but I didn't {{give in}}.
drill.hint: stop refusing and let her have it (not *cave*)

entries.related: *cave (in)* — informal, give in under pressure; *back down* — stop insisting on your position; *give up* — stop trying.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To deal with a problem, a confusing situation or a mess so that it is solved or organized.
entries.usage: Common in speech: *sort out a problem, the paperwork, a mess*, and *things will sort themselves out*. A noun object can go before or after *out*; a pronoun goes in the middle: *Let me sort it out.* It is especially frequent in British English, but Americans use it too, alongside *work out* and *straighten out*.
entries.pattern: sort out a problem / a mix-up / the paperwork; sort it out
examples: I spent all morning on the phone trying to **sort out** a problem with my health insurance.
You two need to **sort** this **out** without yelling at each other.
Before the movers come, we need to **sort out** the garage.

drill.sentence: Our internet bill was wrong for three months, but one call to customer service {{sorted it out}}.
drill.hint: got the problem solved (not *fixed it* or *straightened it out*)

entries.related: *work out* — find a solution by thinking or talking; *straighten out* — fix a confused situation; *figure out* — understand or solve.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make other people understand an idea, a message or a feeling, especially when this is not easy.
entries.usage: Common in talk about teaching, ads, speeches and arguments: *get your point across*, *get the message across*. The object usually goes in the middle, and *to* + the audience can follow: *get it across to the kids*. It focuses on whether the listener understood, not on how well you spoke.
entries.pattern: get your point / the message / an idea across (to someone)
examples: She's a great teacher because she can **get** difficult ideas **across** in simple words.
I tried to **get** my point **across**, but he kept interrupting me.
The ad **gets** its message **across** in under ten seconds, without a single word.

drill.sentence: The safety video uses cartoons to {{get the message across}} to young kids.
drill.hint: make the main point understood (not *convey* or *communicate* it)

entries.related: *convey* — formal; *put across* — very similar; *come across* — be understood, or seem a certain way: *Her message came across clearly.*

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To receive a reply from a person or organization you have contacted, applied to or asked something.
entries.usage: Very common with jobs, applications, landlords and offices: *I'll let you know when I hear back.* It is intransitive; add *from* + the person or organization, and *about* or *on* for the topic. It is often negative and in the present perfect: *We still haven't heard back from them.*
entries.pattern: hear back (from someone) (about something)
examples: I had a great interview on Monday, and they said I'd **hear back** within a few days.
Did you ever **hear back from** the vet about Max's blood test?
We'll start the repairs as soon as we **hear back from** the insurance company.

drill.sentence: I emailed three plumbers on Monday, and I still haven't {{heard back}} from any of them.
drill.hint: gotten a reply (two words)

entries.related: *get back to someone* — the other side: reply to someone (*I'll get back to you*); *hear from someone* — get any message from them, not only a reply.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To register or put your name on a list to join a course, service, event or activity.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday speech and on websites: *sign up for a class, a free trial, the newsletter*. It is intransitive; the thing follows *for*, and *sign up to* + verb also works: *I signed up to volunteer.* To register another person, put them in the middle: *I signed the kids up for swim lessons.*
entries.pattern: sign up for + noun; sign up to + verb; sign someone up
examples: I just **signed up for** a pottery class at the community center.
If you **sign up** before Friday, your first month is free.
Over two hundred people have **signed up** to run in the charity race.

drill.sentence: Registration closes tonight, so {{sign up}} now if you want a spot in the beginners' swim class.
drill.hint: put your name on the list (not *register* or *enroll*)

mistake.wrong: I signed in for a yoga class at the gym.
mistake.right: I signed up for a yoga class at the gym.
mistake.why: *Sign up* means register for something; *sign in* means log in to an account or record that you have arrived.

entries.related: *enroll in* — more formal, for courses and programs; *register for* — neutral and official; *sign on* — agree to join a project or job.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To continue doing something at the same good level, or to continue a good habit or effort without stopping.
entries.usage: Very common as praise: *Keep it up!*, *Keep up the good work.* A noun object can go before or after *up*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *keep it up*. Don't confuse it with *keep up (with someone)*, which means move or learn as fast as others.
entries.pattern: keep up the good work / the pace; keep it up
examples: Your Spanish is getting so much better. **Keep it up**!
If he **keeps up** this pace, he'll finish the marathon in under three hours.
We started walking after dinner in January, and we've **kept** it **up** all year.

drill.sentence: You've practiced piano every day for a month. If you {{keep it up}}, you'll be ready for the recital.
drill.hint: continue at this level (not *stick with it*)

entries.related: *maintain* — more formal; *stick with something* — not give up; *keep up with someone* — go as fast as someone else.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To complete a form, an application or a survey by writing the required information in it.
entries.usage: The usual American phrase; British speakers more often say *fill in* a form. A noun object can go before or after *out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *fill it out*. Americans do say *fill in*, but mostly for single blanks or missing details: *fill in the blanks*.
entries.pattern: fill out a form / an application / a survey; fill it out
examples: Before you can adopt a dog from the shelter, you have to **fill out** a four-page application.
I **filled out** about thirty job applications before I got a single interview.
If you **fill out** a short survey, you get ten percent off your next order.

drill.sentence: Before your first appointment, please {{fill out}} the patient forms online.
drill.hint: complete with your details (the usual American phrase)

entries.related: *fill in* — British for forms; in American English, add missing details: *fill in the blanks*; *complete* — formal, common on official forms.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To go to someone or something for help, advice or comfort when you are in a difficult situation.
entries.usage: Common in talk about hard times: *She had no one to turn to.* The person or thing follows *to*, and *for* + what you need is often added: *turn to your parents for money*. The object can also be an activity or a habit used for comfort: *turn to music, food, alcohol*.
entries.pattern: turn to someone (for help / advice / support)
examples: When I got the diagnosis, my best friend was the first person I **turned to**.
Many people **turn to** online forums for advice about their health.
After his wife died, he **turned to** painting to get through the long evenings.

drill.sentence: She moved to a new city where she knew nobody, so she had no one to {{turn to}} when things got hard.
drill.hint: go to for help and support (not *rely on*, *lean on* or *count on*)

entries.related: *rely on* — depend on regularly; *lean on* — informal, depend on for emotional support; *confide in* — tell your secrets or worries to.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To mention or show something as evidence for a claim, or as the likely cause of something.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and arguments: *Experts point to rising costs.* The subject can be a person who cites the evidence, or the evidence itself, which suggests a conclusion: *The data point to a clear trend.* Use *to*, not *at*, in this abstract sense; *point at* is for pointing with your finger.
entries.pattern: point to + evidence / a cause; point to X as the reason
examples: When asked why sales fell, the owner **pointed to** the road construction outside the store.
Several studies **point to** a link between loneliness and heart disease.
All the evidence **points to** the same conclusion: the fire started in the kitchen.

drill.sentence: Fans and coaches {{point to}} injuries as the main reason the team missed the playoffs.
drill.hint: name as the evidence or cause (not *cite* or *blame*)

entries.related: *cite* — formal, name as evidence; *suggest* — what evidence does more cautiously; *point out* — tell someone a fact they may not have noticed.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To demand publicly that something happen or be done.
entries.usage: Common in news: groups, experts, parents and editorials *call for* changes, an investigation, calm or a ban. The object is a noun or *someone to do something*: *call for the company to recall the product*. It is inseparable; *call for* also means require (*The recipe calls for two eggs*), which is a different sense.
entries.pattern: call for + noun; call for someone to do something
examples: Parents are **calling for** a crosswalk outside the elementary school after two near misses.
Fans are **calling for** the coach to be fired after the team's tenth straight loss.
Doctors have **called for** clearer warning labels on energy drinks.

drill.sentence: After two dog bites in the park this summer, neighbors are {{calling for}} a stricter leash law.
drill.hint: publicly and strongly asking for (not *demanding* or *pushing for*)

entries.related: *demand* — stronger and more direct; *urge* — strongly advise; *push for* — work actively to get something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop thinking or worrying about something from the past, such as anger, guilt or a hope, so that it no longer controls you.
entries.usage: Common in advice, therapy and talk about relationships: *let go of the past, anger, a grudge, regrets*. The object follows *of*, and *let go* alone also works: *You need to let go.* Don't confuse it with *let someone go*, which can mean fire someone.
entries.pattern: let go of the past / anger / a grudge / someone
examples: It took me years to **let go of** the anger I felt toward my father.
At some point, you have to **let go of** the idea that everyone will like you.
She finally **let go of** her dream of playing professional soccer and went to nursing school.

drill.sentence: The breakup was two years ago. It's time to {{let go of}} him and move on with your life.
drill.hint: stop holding on emotionally to (not *get over*)

entries.related: *get over* — recover from a loss or a breakup; *move on* — start a new stage after something ends; *hold on to* — the opposite, keep a feeling or memory.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make someone feel very worried, tense and nervous.
entries.usage: Informal and very common in speech: *Traffic stresses me out.* The person goes in the middle, especially a pronoun, and the adjective *stressed out* is even more common: *I'm so stressed out.* Without an object, *stress out* means become stressed: *Don't stress out about it.*
entries.pattern: X stresses someone out; be / get stressed out
examples: Driving downtown at rush hour really **stresses** me **out**.
My mom was so **stressed out** about the move that she couldn't sleep.
Don't tell him about the lineup change yet. It'll just **stress** him **out** before the big game.

drill.sentence: Planning the wedding has been {{stressing her out}} so much that she's thinking of eloping.
drill.hint: making her tense and anxious (not *getting to her*)

mistake.why: With a pronoun object, the pronoun must go between *stress* and *out*.

entries.related: *stress* alone works too: *Don't stress.*; *freak someone out* — scare or upset someone badly; *get to someone* — slowly annoy or upset them.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To choose or accept a particular option, plan or suggestion.
entries.usage: Very common in speech when deciding or ordering: *I'll go with the salmon*, *Let's go with your idea.* It is inseparable and sounds casual and decisive; in formal writing people say *choose* or *opt for*. *Go with your gut* means trust your instinct.
entries.pattern: go with an option / a plan / someone's idea
examples: We looked at five apartments and decided to **go with** the one near the park.
"What can I get you?" "I think I'll **go with** the soup of the day."
The library board **went with** the cheaper design for the new children's wing.

drill.sentence: Both quotes were close, so we {{went with}} the contractor who could start next week.
drill.hint: chose, in casual speech (not *picked* or *hired*)

entries.related: *go for* — choose, often something you want or like; *opt for* — formal; *settle on* — finally choose after thinking.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To visit a person or place briefly and informally, often without arranging it first.
entries.usage: Common and friendly: *Feel free to drop by anytime.* It works alone or with a place (*drop by the office*, *drop by my place*), and *to* + verb gives the reason: *drop by to say hi*. *Stop by* and *swing by* mean almost the same; *drop in (on someone)* stresses that the visit is unannounced.
entries.pattern: drop by (someone's place / the office) (to say hi)
examples: My neighbor **dropped by** this morning with a plate of cookies.
If you're ever in Austin, **drop by**. We'd love to see you.
A few old coworkers **dropped by** the hospital to see Dad after his surgery.

drill.sentence: We were just about to eat when my in-laws {{dropped by}} without calling first.
drill.hint: came for a short, unplanned visit (not *showed up*, *came by* or *stopped by*; the particle is not *in*)

entries.related: *stop by* — very similar, often on the way somewhere; *drop in (on someone)* — visit without warning; *come over* — visit someone's home, not necessarily briefly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To visit a place or person briefly, usually on the way to somewhere else.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and emails: *stop by the store, the office, my desk*, *Stop by anytime.* It takes a place directly (*stop by the bank*) or works alone, often with *on the way* or *to* + verb: *I'll stop by to pick up the keys.* British speakers more often say *pop in* or *call in*.
entries.pattern: stop by + place; stop by (on the way) to + verb
examples: The neighbors **stopped by** with a pie the day we moved in.
Feel free to **stop by** my office if you have questions about the assignment.
We **stopped by** a little winery on the drive back from the coast.

drill.sentence: I'll {{stop by}} the post office on my way to work and mail your package.
drill.hint: make a quick visit to (not *drop by* or *swing by*; the particle is not *at*)

entries.related: *drop by* — similar, more often a social visit; *swing by* — informal, a quick detour; *stop off* — make a short stop during a trip.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To continue doing something, especially after an interruption or in spite of a difficulty.
entries.usage: Common as a polite phrase (*Please carry on*) and with *with* + noun: *carry on with the meeting*. Americans also *carry on a tradition* (keep it alive), but for simple continuing they usually prefer *keep going*, *keep* + *-ing* or *go on*. It is more frequent in British English, so in casual American speech it can sound slightly British.
entries.pattern: carry on (with something); carry on a tradition
examples: Sorry to interrupt. Please **carry on**.
Despite the rain, the band **carried on** and played for another hour.
After her grandmother died, she **carried on** the family tradition of making tamales every Christmas.

drill.sentence: The power went out for a minute, but the teacher just {{carried on}} with the lesson in the dark.
drill.hint: continued without stopping (not *went on* or *kept going*)

entries.related: *keep going* — the most common everyday choice; *go on* — continue, also continue talking; *resume* — formal, start again after a pause.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To take action to handle a problem, task or difficult person, or to cope with a difficult situation.
entries.usage: Extremely common in all registers: *deal with a complaint, stress, the kids*. It is inseparable (*I'll deal with it*), and the past form is *dealt* /dɛlt/. In speech, *I can't deal with this right now* means you are too tired or upset to handle it.
entries.pattern: deal with a problem / a complaint / stress / someone
examples: Customer service **dealt with** my complaint in under ten minutes.
I'll **deal with** the dishes later; right now I need a nap.
How do you **deal with** stress when everything happens at once?

drill.sentence: The kitchen sink has been leaking for a week, and my husband keeps saying he'll {{deal with}} it tomorrow.
drill.hint: take action about (not *handle*, *fix* or *take care of*)

entries.related: *handle* — very similar, often about skill; *cope with* — get through a hard situation emotionally; *tackle* — start dealing with a big problem.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To cause something to happen as a result, often after a series of steps or over time.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, news and academic writing: *lead to problems, delays, a fight, better results*. It is inseparable, and *to* is a preposition, so it takes a noun or an *-ing* form, never a bare verb. The past form is *led* /lɛd/.
entries.pattern: X leads to + noun / -ing
examples: One small argument about money **led to** a week of silence.
Heavy rain overnight **led to** flooding on several roads.
Starting school an hour later has **led to** better attendance in several districts.

drill.sentence: Too much screen time before bed can {{lead to}} poor sleep.
drill.hint: bring about as a consequence (not *cause*, *result in* or *contribute to*)

mistake.wrong: Skipping breakfast can lead to eat more later.
mistake.right: Skipping breakfast can lead to eating more later.
mistake.why: *To* in *lead to* is a preposition, so it takes a noun or an *-ing* form.

entries.related: *result in* — similar, more formal; *cause* — more direct; *lead someone to do something* — make someone do something: *What led you to quit?*

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To depend on someone or something for help or support, and trust that they will be there.
entries.usage: Common in all registers: *rely on friends, the bus, a car, coffee*. It is inseparable, and you can add *for* + noun or *to* + verb: *rely on her for advice*, *rely on him to pick up the kids*. *Count on* is more informal and stresses trust; *depend on* is a close synonym.
entries.pattern: rely on someone (for something / to do something)
examples: My grandmother **relies on** her neighbors to bring her groceries.
We don't have a car, so we **rely on** the bus to get everywhere.
You can always **rely on** Sam. He's never once let me down.

drill.sentence: As a single dad, he has to {{rely on}} his parents to watch the kids after school.
drill.hint: trust for regular help (not *depend on*, *count on* or *lean on*)

entries.related: *depend on* — very similar; *count on* — informal, trust someone to do something; *lean on* — depend on for emotional support.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To cause a particular outcome or effect; the subject is the cause and the object is the result.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in news, reports and academic writing: *result in delays, injuries, a fine*. It takes a noun or an *-ing* form; in casual speech people more often say *lead to* or *cause*. Don't mix it up with *result from*, where the subject is the effect: *The delay resulted from a power outage.*
entries.pattern: cause + results in + effect; effect + results from + cause
examples: The power outage at the airport **resulted in** hundreds of canceled flights.
Late payments can **result in** a fee of up to forty dollars.
The crash on the interstate **resulted in** two injuries and a three-hour traffic jam.

drill.sentence: Leaving the stove on while you're out could {{result in}} a serious fire.
drill.hint: end up causing (not *lead to* or *cause*)

mistake.wrong: The flooding resulted in heavy rain.
mistake.right: The flooding resulted from heavy rain.
mistake.why: *Result in* goes from the cause to the effect; *result from* goes from the effect back to the cause.

entries.related: *lead to* — similar, more common in speech; *cause* — more direct; *result from* — the reverse direction.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To have a friendly relationship with someone and not argue much.
entries.usage: The usual American phrase; British speakers often say *get on (with someone)*. It is intransitive; add *with* + the person, or use a plural subject: *My sister and I get along great.* It is often used with *well*, *great* or *really*, and in the negative: *They don't get along.*
entries.pattern: get along (well / great) (with someone)
examples: My two cats didn't **get along** at first, but now they sleep curled up together.
I **get along** really well with my coworkers, which makes the long hours easier.
Do you **get along with** your in-laws, or are the holidays a little tense?

drill.sentence: My roommate and I {{get along}} great. We've never had a single fight.
drill.hint: have a friendly relationship (not *click* or the British *get on*)

entries.related: *get on* — the British equivalent; *hit it off* — like each other immediately; *see eye to eye* — agree.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To admire and respect someone, often someone older or more experienced, and want to be like them.
entries.usage: Common when talking about parents, older siblings, coaches, teachers and athletes: *Kids look up to him.* It is inseparable, and the person comes after *to*. The opposite is *look down on someone*, which means feel that you are better than them.
entries.pattern: look up to a parent / a coach / an older sibling
examples: My little brother **looks up to** me, so I try to set a good example.
Young players **look up to** her because she came from the same small town.
I've always **looked up to** my grandfather. He built his business from nothing.

drill.sentence: Kids {{look up to}} famous athletes, so athletes should think about how they behave in public.
drill.hint: respect and want to be like (not *admire* or *idolize*)

entries.related: *admire* — more general; *idolize* — admire too much, without seeing faults; *look down on* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To give finished work, a document or something you found to the person or office in charge of it.
entries.usage: Common at school and work in American English: *turn in homework, a report, your keys*; British speakers more often say *hand in*. A noun object can go before or after *in*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *turn it in*. *Turn someone in* means report them to the police.
entries.pattern: turn in homework / a report / your badge; turn it in
examples: Please **turn in** your essays by Friday at noon.
On your last day, you'll need to **turn in** your laptop and your badge.
Someone found my wallet at the gym and **turned it in** at the front desk.

drill.sentence: Make sure you {{turn in}} your homework before the bell rings, or Mr. Lopez won't accept it.
drill.hint: give to the teacher (not *hand in* or *submit*)

entries.related: *hand in* — same, more common in British English; *submit* — formal, common for online forms and applications; *turn in* with no object — informal, go to bed.

entries.label: phrasal verb (passive)
entries.meaning: To dislike something or someone, or lose interest in them, because of a particular feature or behavior.
entries.usage: Common in reviews and conversation: *I was put off by the price, the smell, his attitude.* It is usually passive with *by*; the active form puts the cause first: *The long lines put me off.* The adjective *off-putting* is also common, and Americans often say *be turned off by* in the same sense.
entries.pattern: be put off by + noun; X puts someone off
examples: We were **put off by** the rude host and ended up eating somewhere else.
Some buyers are **put off by** the house's tiny kitchen.
Don't be **put off by** the long name; the dish is basically fried rice.

drill.sentence: I almost didn't read the book because I was {{put off}} by the cover, but it turned out to be great.
drill.hint: made to dislike it at first (not *turned off*)

entries.related: *be turned off by* — similar, common in American speech; *off-putting* — unpleasant in a way that pushes people away; *put something off* — a different verb: postpone.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To make sure that someone is safe and well, or to check that they are doing what they should.
entries.usage: It can sound caring (*check up on an elderly neighbor*) or controlling (*My boss keeps checking up on me*), depending on context. It is inseparable; *check on someone* means almost the same and sounds more neutral. The noun *checkup* is a routine medical exam.
entries.pattern: check up on someone
examples: Our neighbor is ninety, so we stop by most mornings to **check up on** her.
Are you **checking up on** me? I said I'd finish the report by noon.
A social worker **checks up on** the foster family at least once a month.

drill.sentence: My mom texts me every hour when I'm out with friends, just to {{check up on}} me.
drill.hint: make sure I'm safe and behaving (three words; not *keep tabs on*)

entries.related: *check on* — more neutral and caring; *keep tabs on* — informal, watch someone closely; *look in on* — visit briefly to see if someone is OK.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make a process or activity happen faster, or, without an object, to start moving faster.
entries.usage: Common in everyday talk and business: *speed up the process, delivery, a slow computer*. A noun object can go before or after *up*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *speed it up*. Without an object it means go faster (*The car sped up*), and the usual past form is *sped up*.
entries.pattern: speed up the process / delivery; speed it up
examples: Is there any way to **speed up** my refund? I returned the jacket three weeks ago.
Can you **speed it up** a little? We're going to miss the train.
The city added bus lanes on Main Street to **speed up** the morning commute.

drill.sentence: Paying an extra fee will {{speed up}} your passport renewal, but it still takes about two weeks.
drill.hint: make faster (not *expedite* or *fast-track*)

entries.related: *hurry up* — mostly to tell a person to go faster; *expedite* — formal, for orders and documents; *slow down* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To discuss a problem, plan or decision with someone, usually calmly and in detail, before you decide.
entries.usage: Common in families, couples and at work: *Let me talk it over with my wife.* The object usually goes in the middle, especially a pronoun (*talk it over*), and *with* + the person is often added. It is also a polite way to delay a decision, like *think it over*.
entries.pattern: talk it / things over (with someone)
examples: I got a job offer in Seattle, but I want to **talk it over** with my family first.
We **talked** things **over** for a whole weekend and decided to sell the house.
Let's grab coffee and **talk over** the plans for Mom's sixtieth birthday.

drill.sentence: We don't have to decide tonight. Let's sleep on it and {{talk it over}} in the morning.
drill.hint: discuss it together (not *go over it*)

entries.related: *think something over* — consider it alone before deciding; *discuss* — neutral, more formal; *talk something through* — discuss step by step to understand it.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To make plans or arrangements in advance, thinking about what will happen later.
entries.usage: Common in advice about travel, money, meals and busy periods: *If you plan ahead, you'll save money.* It is intransitive; add *for* + an event or period: *plan ahead for retirement, the holidays*. The informal opposite is *wing it*: do something without preparing.
entries.pattern: plan ahead (for something)
examples: Holiday flights sell out fast, so if you don't **plan ahead**, you'll pay a fortune.
I **plan ahead** and cook all my lunches for the week on Sunday.
Several roads downtown will be closed this weekend, so drivers should **plan ahead**.

drill.sentence: If you want a campsite at Yosemite in July, you really need to {{plan ahead}}.
drill.hint: arrange things well in advance (not *book early*)

entries.related: *think ahead* — consider future problems; *prepare* — get ready; *wing it* — informal, do something without preparing.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To leave home or work and go somewhere for a short vacation or a rest.
entries.usage: Common in conversation: *We're trying to get away for the weekend*, *I just need to get away.* It is intransitive; add *for* + a period or *to* + a place. The noun *getaway* is common in travel ads: *a weekend getaway*.
entries.pattern: get away (for the weekend / to the beach)
examples: Work has been crazy lately. I really need to **get away** for a few days.
Every summer, my parents **get away** to a little cabin on the lake.
We're hoping to **get away** for a long weekend in October, just the two of us.

drill.sentence: With the kids at summer camp, we finally had a chance to {{get away}} for three days in Maine.
drill.hint: leave home for a short break (not *take off*; the verb is not *go*)

entries.related: *get away from it all* — escape your normal stress; *take a break* — stop working for a while; *getaway* — the noun, a short vacation.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become lower in price, level or amount.
entries.usage: Common for prices, rates, fevers, numbers and temperatures: *Rents are finally coming down.* It is intransitive; add *to* for the new level and *by* for the amount: *came down by ten percent*. In bargaining, a seller can *come down* too: *Can you come down a little on the price?*
entries.pattern: prices / rates / a fever come(s) down (to … / by …)
examples: Egg prices have finally **come down**, so I'm making omelets again.
Her fever **came down** overnight, and she's eating again.
The seller wouldn't **come down** on the price, so we walked away.

drill.sentence: Mortgage rates have {{come down}} a little this month, so it might be a good time to refinance.
drill.hint: become lower (not *dropped*, *fallen* or *eased*; the verb is not *gone*)

entries.related: *go down* — very similar; *drop* — fall, often quickly; *go up* — the opposite.
